transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I just don’t feel like myself anymore. I used to hike, coach, play guitar, keep up with people, and now I don’t really do any of it. I don’t call people back. Some days I’m just sitting in my rental for hours, knowing there are things I should do, but I can’t get myself to start.
How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, months, or longer?
Longer. It’s been... about a year and two months, I think. Things started unraveling after I moved into that smaller rental after the divorce.
Over these past 14 months, has your mood and lack of motivation stayed pretty much the same the whole time, or have there been stretches where it got noticeably worse or better?

It’s been mostly the same, I’d say. Maybe some days are a little worse than others, but overall it’s just this steady feeling like I’m not myself. I don’t hike, I stopped coaching, I barely touch the guitar, and I don’t call people back. Some days I’ll just sit there in that rental for hours, knowing I should do something, and I just can’t get started.
During this past year or so, have you also noticed changes in your sleep or appetite, trouble concentrating, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, or any thoughts of not wanting to be alive?

I’m not sure. I mean, my focus isn’t great, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing. Sleep and appetite… I haven’t really kept track. I don’t think I’ve been noticing those things clearly. And thoughts about not wanting to be alive—no, I don’t really know how to answer that beyond saying I haven’t been focused on that.
Over the past year, have you noticed any change in how much or how well you're sleeping compared to before—like trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t been keeping track of my sleep, and nothing stands out to me clearly, like a big change one way or the other. Some nights feel off, but I can’t say if it’s more or less than before.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite or your weight over the past year—eating more or less than you used to, or gaining or losing weight without trying?
I don’t really know. I haven’t been watching my weight, and I can’t say I’ve noticed a clear change in how much I eat. Nothing stands out to me like gaining or losing a lot without trying.
Over this past year, have you found yourself feeling worthless, or blaming yourself excessively for things, more than you used to?
I don’t think so. I mean, I get frustrated with myself sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed feeling worthless or blaming myself all the time more than before.
Over this past year, have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy nearly every day, even without much physical activity?
I’m not really sure. I have days where I feel worn out, but I can’t say it’s been nearly every day or clearly different from before. Nothing really stands out to me that way.
Would you say your trouble focusing or making decisions happens nearly every day, or is it more occasional and mild?
I’m not really sure. I lose focus sometimes, but I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed it happening nearly every day. It feels more like it comes and goes.
Would you say that this loss of interest in things like hiking, coaching, or playing guitar has been present nearly every day over the past year, or does it come and go?

It’s more like it’s there most days, yeah. I just don’t feel like myself anymore. I stopped hiking, stopped coaching, don’t really play guitar, and I don’t call people back like I should. Some days I just sit in my rental for hours knowing there are things I need to do, but I can’t get myself to start.

Over this past year, has this affected your ability to function at work or in your daily responsibilities, or have you mostly still been able to keep up with your basic obligations despite feeling this way?

Yeah, it’s affected things a lot. I got suspended from my protective service job after a routine patrol where I scared some staff and people nearby. Since then I’ve kind of pulled back from everything—coaching, volunteering, even people who used to rely on me. I’m not really keeping up like I used to.
Aside from losing interest in things, have you been feeling sad, down, or depressed nearly every day over this past year?
I don’t know if I’d call it depressed nearly every day. I’ve felt off and not like myself, but sad or down every single day… I’m not sure. I haven’t really been tracking it that way.

Looking back over this past year, was there ever a stretch of at least two weeks where you felt distinctly worse—like your mood, sleep, appetite, and energy all dropped together—compared to how you've been feeling generally?

I’m not sure. I can’t really point to a clear two-week stretch where everything dropped together like that. It’s been more like… a steady bad stretch overall, with some days worse than others, but I haven’t noticed a specific period like you’re describing.
Over this past year, would you say you've felt down or low in mood on more days than not, even if not every single day?
I’m not really sure. I’ve had a lot of bad days, but I don’t know if I’d say I felt low more days than not. It’s hard for me to separate “low mood” from just feeling off and not myself.
Before the divorce and the move into the rental about 14 months ago, do you think you were already starting to feel this way, or did this really begin around that time?
It really seemed to begin around then. After the divorce, when I moved into that smaller rental, things just started unraveling. That was about a year and two months ago.
I’m sorry, I’m not sure what you’re asking me right now. Could you repeat the question?
Since that incident on patrol where you scared people, have you been having any unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about it, or found yourself feeling unusually on edge or easily startled?
I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve had flashbacks or nightmares about it, not that I can remember. I do feel tense sometimes, but I can’t say it’s specifically because of that patrol incident.
Over this past year, have people noticed you moving, speaking, or reacting more slowly than usual, or on the other hand, have you felt unusually restless or fidgety, nearly every day?

Yeah… people did notice. On patrol I started reacting before I could slow myself down. I’d crouch behind counters, signal people to get back, repeat the last thing they said to see if it meant something, and I’d pace the same route over and over. Staff started looking scared of me.

Since that day on patrol, have you noticed yourself doing similar things—like being unusually watchful, repeating what people say, or feeling on edge—in other situations since then, or was that mainly limited to that one incident?

It wasn’t just that one moment, no. The patrol was when it got really obvious. I’d react before I could think—ducking behind counters, waving people back, repeating what they just said because I thought maybe it meant something, and then pacing the same route again and again. People started looking scared of me, and that’s when I realized it wasn’t normal.

When you found yourself repeating what people said or feeling like it might 'mean something,' can you tell me more about that—did you feel like there were hidden messages or special meanings in ordinary things, or did you see or hear anything unusual that others didn't seem to notice?

Yeah. I mean… I know it sounds extreme, but it felt like ordinary things weren’t ordinary. For months I was sure the guys across from my rental, and some people at work, were tracking my patrol routes or checking my locks somehow.

It was things like the same cars showing up, or little comments people made that seemed to line up too perfectly with what I’d just done. It didn’t feel random to me. It felt like they were sending signals or testing me.

doctor.question: Over this past year, have people noticed you moving, speaking, or reacting more slowly than usual, or on the other hand, have you felt unusually restless or fidgety, nearly every day?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: On patrol I started reacting before I could slow myself down, like crouching behind counters, signaling people to get back, repeating their last words to check if they were part of it, and pacing the same route until staff looked scared of me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in movement, speech, reactions, restlessness, or fidgeting, which most directly relates to abnormal or disturbed behavior and motor activity.

patient.answer: Yeah… people did notice. On patrol I started reacting before I could slow myself down. I’d crouch behind counters, signal people to get back, repeat the last thing they said to see if it meant something, and I’d pace the same route over and over. Staff started looking scared of me.

inference.note: The description of crouching, signaling, repeating phrases, and pacing repetitive routes during patrol suggests hyperarousal/hypervigilance and exaggerated startle-type behaviors, raising concern for PTSD (F43.1) related to occupational trauma, in addition to the chronic depressive picture. Criteria for full MDD remain unmet due to lack of clear symptom clustering, so F32.9 and F34.1 remain considerations pending further clarification.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the hypervigilant, repetitive behaviors seen during the patrol incident have continued or recurred since then, which would support ongoing PTSD-type hyperarousal rather than an isolated event
doctor.question: Since that day on patrol, have you noticed yourself doing similar things—like being unusually watchful, repeating what people say, or feeling on edge—in other situations since then, or was that mainly limited to that one incident?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: On patrol I started reacting before I could slow myself down, like crouching behind counters, signaling people to get back, repeating their last words to check if they were part of it, and pacing the same route until staff looked scared of me.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the unusual patrol behaviors—being watchful, repeating what people say, and reacting in odd or inappropriate ways—continued in other situations, which directly matches the disorganized/abnormal behavior profile.

patient.answer: It wasn’t just that one moment, no. The patrol was when it got really obvious. I’d react before I could think—ducking behind counters, waving people back, repeating what they just said because I thought maybe it meant something, and then pacing the same route again and again. People started looking scared of me, and that’s when I realized it wasn’t normal.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychotic features (referential thinking, paranoia, perceptual disturbances) underlying the odd behaviors during patrol
doctor.question: When you found yourself repeating what people said or feeling like it might 'mean something,' can you tell me more about that—did you feel like there were hidden messages or special meanings in ordinary things, or did you see or hear anything unusual that others didn't seem to notice?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds extreme, but for months I've been certain the guys across from my rental and some people at work were tracking my patrol routes and testing my locks, because the same cars and little comments kept lining up too perfectly to be random.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether ordinary things felt like hidden messages or special meanings, which most directly relates to fixed unusual beliefs.

patient.answer:
Yeah. I mean… I know it sounds extreme, but it felt like ordinary things weren’t ordinary. For months I was sure the guys across from my rental, and some people at work, were tracking my patrol routes or checking my locks somehow.

It was things like the same cars showing up, or little comments people made that seemed to line up too perfectly with what I’d just done. It didn’t feel random to me. It felt like they were sending signals or testing me.

inference.note: Added psychotic-spectrum disorders given clear paranoid/referential delusions (belief of being tracked/tested) and catatonic-like behaviors (crouching, echoing speech, repetitive pacing) that emerged over a chronic course; depressive/negative symptoms persist but do not meet full major depressive episode criteria, making unipolar depression less likely as primary diagnosis. PTSD less supported given no flashbacks/nightmares tied to trauma.
